body_markdown:
While it may have the least playful-sounding name ever, the Specialty Equipment Market Association (SEMA) show is one we get excited about every year. Founded in 1967 to help small businesses in the automotive aftermarket, it has also attracted the companies that make the vehicles that customers modify using parts from said small businesses. If you want to know what the car people at a given OEM are thinking about, watch SEMA. Case in point: Nissan, whose three SEMA builds indicate that it houses some serious racing fans.


Exhibit A: The Nissan Project NAT2 SCCA Touring 2. It draws on the brand’s impressive track record in the Sports Car Club of America (SCCA), a lineage that lives on even in the stock Z, which[reminded us of an SCCA showroom-stock car](https://www.hagerty.com/media/new-car-reviews/first-look-review-2023-nissan-z/) . Nissan started racing in the SCCA for marketing purposes in the ’60s via its Datsun brand, which had only started selling cars here in 1958. It didn’t take long for Datsuns to prove their worth on track. By 1967, a 1600 had claimed the brand’s first championship. Thanks to extensive trackside support from Nissan, their numbers and victories multiplied. Decades later, Nissan became the very first brand in SCCA racing to achieve 100 victories at the Runoffs, the SCCA’s annual, multi-class championship event.


Nissan/Bradley Mansour


Nissan


Nissan


Nissan


This 2026 SEMA build is tailored to SCCA’s Touring 2 class, which includes familiar faces like the Ford Mustang, Chevrolet Corvette, and BMW M2CS. The Z’s driveline has been transformed for racing with a cold-air intake kit, a NISMO-designed stainless-steel exhaust, an upgraded radiator and heat exchanger, race-grade fluids, and a differential cooler kit from Z1 Motorsports, which also developed a custom engine tune.[Per the SCCA’s rules](https://cdn.connectsites.net/user_files/scca/downloads/000/079/210/APR-26.pdf?1774985839) for the Z, the twin-turbo V-6 wears 38mm restrictors on the inlets of the turbochargers. The suspension has been fed a steady diet of polyurethane (excepting the subframe bushings, also from Z1, which are aluminum) and thoroughly upgraded with NISMO coilovers, front upper control arms, sway bars on both ends, and an adjustable sway bar end link. The brakes have been upgraded with Z1’s Track Big Brake Kit, including stainless steel lines front and rear, and Hawk DTC-60 pads.


The red, white, and blue livery on this build harkens to a name closely associated with Datsuns and Nissans,[Brock Racing Enterprises](https://www.hagerty.com/media/people/how-peter-brock-beat-odds-and-carroll-shelby-with-a-hino/) . Founded by[Pete Brock](https://www.hagerty.com/media/never-stop-driving/never-stop-driving-171-pete-brock-the-interview/) and backed by Nissan’s Japanese arm, BRE earned C Production National Championships in 1970 and 1971.


Nissan/Bradley Mansour


Inside, the Z has been stripped to bare metal—goodbye HVAC system, stereo, and windows. It’s been reinforced with a full SCCA competition-spec rollcage and equipped with a Sabelt six-point harness, bucket seat, and flat-bottom steering wheel. Shifting duties are now handled by a paddle-shifter kit from Zestek. Our kudos to the racing-obsessed Nissan employees who developed this car. It looks like it could be competitive right out of the box.


Nissan/John Murphy


Nissan/John Murphy


Nissan/John Murphy


Nissan


Nissan/John Murphy


Exhibits B and C look back to more Nissan motorsports heritage. The Nissan Sentra Spec-V Concept celebrates 35 years since the first Sentra to bear the Spec-V name. That 1991 sports sedan, with its 16-valve, twin-cam four-cylinder, agile handling, and roomy interior, was enough to make *Car and Driver*[think of the BMW 2002](https://www.caranddriver.com/reviews/a39571978/1991-nissan-sentra-se-r-by-the-numbers/) . The concept built for SEMA is far racier than either of those vehicles, with an aggressive stance and side-exiting exhaust, not to mention a manual transmission swapped from the Nissan Juke NISMO RS (remember that crazy thing?). It boasts the brakes, rear spoiler, and Recaro seats from a GT-R, coilovers and anti-roll bars from NISMO, and an engine stuffed with upgraded internals and even supplemental port injection. Nissan really went all-out with this one!


Nissan / Larry Chen


Nissan / Larry Chen


Nissan / Larry Chen


Nissan / Larry Chen


Exhibit C in Nissan’s display of racing enthusiasm is a restomodded Datsun S30 built by longtime brand collaborator Chris Forsberg, who has won three Formula Drift championships, all in Nissans. He and his team are quite familiar with these cars, but they didn’t take the easy way out, swapping a hot-rodded twin-turbo V-6 from the contemporary Z into its forebear—with its six-speed manual transmission, of course. The brakes received an upgrade as well, courtesy of Wilwood, as did the custom suspension, which relies on many parts from Techno Toy. The Seiran Blue paint hides a lot of carbon fiber, used on the front fenders, hood, air dam, bumpers, and hatch.


We are hard-pressed to decide which of these we’d like to borrow for a weekend. We’ll shoot for the stars and wish for a few days on track with the Project NAT2 SCCA Touring 2. Speaking of which, would somebody come up with a cool nickname for this car? For now, we’ll call it Pete.
